summary: Specifies how Deterministic Networking (DetNet) service works for IP traffic on IP hosts and routers. No new DetNet header is defined for IP flows. Instead, existing IP and higher-layer header information is used to identify flows and deliver the service.

eli5.summary: This shows how to give some IP traffic a reserved fast lane without adding a special label, by recognizing the traffic from the address information it already carries.

questions: how does detnet work over ip
how does detnet identify ip flows
does detnet ip provide packet replication
subtitle: How IP routers and hosts give deterministic service to flows by recognizing them from ordinary IP and port fields.

tldr.problem: Deterministic Networking promises extremely low packet loss and assured maximum latency, and the network needs a way to tell which IP packets belong to such a flow.
tldr.mechanism: No DetNet-specific header is added. Nodes match existing IP and transport header fields, mainly the 6-tuple, against provisioned flow information and give matching packets the configured treatment.
tldr.outcome: DetNet service works with unmodified IP packets, but it gives only the forwarding sub-layer, so service protection is per sub-network and not end to end.

today: RFC 8939 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: DetNet Without a New Header
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) is a service a network can offer to flows. It provides extremely low packet loss rates and an assured maximum end-to-end delivery latency. RFC 8939 specifies the data plane for IP hosts and routers that give DetNet service to IP-encapsulated data. It builds on the architecture in RFC 8655 and the data plane framework in RFC 8938.

The architecture splits DetNet data plane functions into a service sub-layer (service protection and reordering) and a forwarding sub-layer (congestion protection). The service sub-layer generally needs extra header fields. Since DetNet IP adds none, only the forwarding sub-layer functions are supported.
sections.eli5: DetNet is a promise that important messages arrive on time and almost never get lost. Here, the promise is kept without adding any new label to the packets.

sections.title: Overview of the IP Data Plane
sections.content:
DetNet nodes follow an end-to-end IP model. Non-DetNet and DetNet IP packets look the same on the wire. The difference is that each DetNet node holds flow-specific information describing the flow and the forwarding behavior it needs. Fields used for flow identification are generally forwarded unmodified, although standard modification of the DSCP field is not precluded.

The data plane mainly uses 6-tuple flow identification: destination address, source address, IP protocol, source port, destination port and DSCP. This is a 5-tuple plus DSCP. Where ports are not available (ICMP, IPsec, ESP) or for aggregates, fewer fields such as a 3-tuple or even a 2-tuple can be used. Optional matching on the IPv6 Flow Label is also allowed.

If end systems are not DetNet aware, edge nodes act as service proxies at the domain boundary and associate the application's IP flows with the right DetNet flow information. The DetNet Controller Plane gives each node the information it needs.
sections.eli5: Routers look at who a packet is from, who it is for, and which program it belongs to. If that matches a reserved list, the packet gets the VIP lane.

sections.title: Domain and End-System Considerations
sections.content:
All nodes along a flow's path need to agree on which fields identify flows. Otherwise flows may interfere with each other or lose the treatment they expect. End systems may be DN attached (connected to an edge node or behind a sub-network) or DN integrated (part of the domain).

DetNet-aware end systems must shape traffic and have buffers to receive it. They should avoid IP fragmentation, because fragments carry no transport headers or port information, so full 6-tuple identification is not possible. The maximum size can be learned through Path MTU Discovery or the Controller Plane. They SHOULD NOT mix DetNet and non-DetNet traffic within a single 5-tuple.

Congestion protection, latency control and resource allocation use link and sub-network mechanisms. Because there is no end-to-end sequencing information, service protection (packet replication and elimination) can only be provided within each link or sub-network, not end to end at the DetNet layer.
sections.eli5: Everyone on the road has to agree on what the VIP sticker looks like. Also, packets should not be chopped into pieces, because the pieces lose the information that shows they are VIP.

sections.title: Forwarding, QoS and Aggregation
sections.content:
Class of Service uses the standard DSCP field. Nodes must make sure that CoS classes do not affect the congestion protection and latency control used for DetNet. Packets that match a DetNet flow whose reservation is incomplete must not use DetNet-allocated resources such as queues or shapers. The RFC suggests treating them as non-DetNet traffic, discarding them, or re-marking their DSCP.

Path selection algorithms are out of scope, but flows may have flow-specific next hops. Using multiple paths such as ECMP for a single DetNet flow is NOT RECOMMENDED, though ECMP MAY be used for non-DetNet flows.

Flows can be aggregated with prefixes, wildcards, lists and ranges to reduce per-hop state. The Controller Plane must ensure aggregated flows have compatible QoS or CoS and that enough resources are allocated, and it MUST ensure that non-congestion-responsive DetNet traffic does not leave the DetNet domain. Bidirectional flows have no special data plane features; co-routing is handled at the management and control level.
sections.eli5: If a packet claims a reserved lane but nobody booked it, the router must not let it use that lane. It can treat it as ordinary traffic, throw it away, or change its label.

sections.title: Flow Identification Procedures
sections.content:
Implementations MUST identify DetNet flows from the fields below, as an end system, relay node or edge node. Flow information MUST be ordered, with a fixed order, and a flow is identified by the first set of matching information.

  • Source and Destination Address: MUST be supported. Longest prefix matching is a SHOULD, and a prefix length of 0 means the field is ignored. Any address value is allowed, including multicast destinations.
  • IPv4 Protocol / IPv6 Next Header: MUST be supported, with the option to ignore it.
  • DSCP: MUST support list-based matching of DSCP values.
  • IPv6 Flow Label: SHOULD be supported, and if supported it MUST be possible to ignore it.
  • TCP and UDP ports: exact-value matching MUST be supported for source and destination ports. Range matching is a SHOULD.
  • ICMP: identified by the protocol number only; the ICMP type is not part of the flow definition.
  • IPsec AH and ESP: exact matching on the Security Parameters Index (SPI) MUST be supported.

Nodes SHALL use management and control information to pick outgoing interfaces and next hops, and must give the flow the traffic treatment provisioned for it, such as queues, buffers, shaping and policing.
sections.eli5: The router has a checklist: sender, receiver, type of traffic, and program door numbers. It goes down its list in order, and the first line that fits decides how the packet is treated.

sections.title: Management and Control Information
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes the information that must be provisioned per DetNet flow through configuration, the Controller Plane or the management plane. It includes the source and destination addresses with prefix lengths, the protocol or next header, whether DSCP is used and its list of values, the optional IPv6 Flow Label, TCP and UDP port values or ranges, the IPsec SPI, and, for end systems, an optional maximum IP packet size.

Implementations MUST support ordering of this information. For example, one specific UDP flow can get its own service while the aggregate of all other flows with the same UDP destination port gets a different one. The Controller Plane is responsible for provisioning both identification information and the resources needed for each flow.
sections.eli5: Somebody has to write the checklist and book the lanes ahead of time. That job belongs to the controller, not to the packets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The data plane adds or modifies no header information. Because there are no DetNet-specific fields, integrity and confidentiality of application flows rely on the underlying technology, for example IPsec for IP flows or MACsec on Ethernet sub-networks.

Per-flow identification at the management and control level may give Controller Plane attackers more information about data flows. The RFC notes this as an inherent property of DetNet to weigh when deciding if DetNet suits a use case. To protect availability, policing and shaping can be applied at the domain input against denial of service, and authentication and authorization of devices can help against delay attacks by man-in-the-middle entities. The RFC considers an attacker who may control a node inside the domain but not its physical links.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is added to the packets, so protection comes from the usual locks. Keeping the booking list private matters, and so does limiting how much traffic enters the fast lane.

viz.caption: THE 6-TUPLE USED TO IDENTIFY A DETNET IP FLOW

items.label: Source address
items.desc: Prefix matching is a SHOULD; length 0 ignores it.

items.label: IP protocol / Next Header
items.desc: May be ignored for a flow.

items.label: Source port
items.desc: TCP or UDP; exact value is a MUST.

items.label: Destination port
items.desc: TCP or UDP; exact value is a MUST.

layers.label: Service sub-layer
layers.detail: Service protection and reordering; not provided by DetNet IP

layers.label: Forwarding sub-layer
layers.detail: Congestion protection; provided by DetNet IP

layers.label: Link / sub-network
layers.detail: For example MPLS or IEEE 802.1 TSN
